name: Career Test
tagline: Find the kind of work that truly fits your interests.
intro: People are happiest at work when their job matches what they naturally enjoy. This test measures six broad work-interest types, from hands-on and investigative to creative, social, enterprising and organised. Rate 100 short statements about activities and preferences. In about five minutes you see your strongest interest area, plus example jobs and work environments that suit you.
seoTitle: Career Test – Find jobs that match your interests
seoDescription: Which career suits you? Take this free 5-minute career interest test and discover your strongest work interests, example jobs and fitting work environments.

realistic.name: Realistic (The Doer)
realistic.short: Interest in hands-on, practical and physical work with tools, machines, nature or animals.
realistic.low: Hands-on, physical work is not what draws you. You probably prefer working with ideas, people or information over tools, machines or the outdoors. That is useful to know: jobs centred on manual or technical labour, such as construction, mechanics or farming, are unlikely to satisfy you for long. When comparing options, look at how much of the day is spent on practical tasks, and favour roles where your main work happens with your mind or with people.
realistic.mid: You have a moderate interest in practical, hands-on work. You enjoy seeing tangible results but probably would not want physical tasks all day. Roles that mix hands-on work with planning, advising or teaching could suit you well, such as lab technician, sports instructor, technical sales, landscape designer or facilities coordinator. Look for workplaces that combine time on site or in a workshop with time at a desk or with clients.
realistic.high: Realistic interests are your strongest area. You like working with your hands, tools, machines, plants or animals, and you value concrete, visible results. Example jobs: electrician, carpenter, mechanic, engineer technician, farmer, forester, chef, pilot, physiotherapist or paramedic. You tend to thrive in practical environments such as workshops, building sites, kitchens or outdoors, in roles where you solve real problems directly. Look for training paths with lots of practice, such as apprenticeships or vocational programmes.

investigative.name: Investigative (The Thinker)
investigative.short: Interest in research, analysis, science and solving complex problems.
investigative.low: Research and analysis are not your main source of motivation. You probably prefer action, people or creative work over studying a problem in depth. Jobs dominated by research, data analysis or scientific study, such as lab scientist or statistician, may feel slow or dry to you. When exploring careers, choose roles where decisions are made quickly and results come from doing rather than investigating, and team up with analytical colleagues when deeper research is needed.
investigative.mid: You have a moderate interest in investigating and analysing. You enjoy figuring things out, but you may not want to spend all day on research. Roles that combine analysis with practical work or people contact can suit you, such as pharmacist, IT support specialist, quality controller, market researcher or medical technician. Look for environments where problem-solving is valued alongside teamwork and visible results.
investigative.high: Investigative interests are your strongest area. You love solving complex problems, understanding how things work and testing ideas against evidence. Example jobs: scientist, doctor, researcher, data analyst, software developer, engineer, psychologist, economist or pharmacologist. You tend to thrive in environments such as universities, laboratories, research and development teams, hospitals or tech companies, in roles that give you independence and intellectual challenge. Seek out projects where depth and accuracy are valued more than speed.

artistic.name: Artistic (The Creator)
artistic.short: Interest in creative expression, design, art, writing and performance.
artistic.low: Creative self-expression is not your main driver at work. You likely prefer clear structures, practical tasks or working with facts and people. Jobs that depend heavily on originality and open-ended creativity, such as artist, designer or writer, may feel unpredictable to you. That gives you clarity: favour roles with defined goals and methods. You can still enjoy creativity as a hobby without needing it to be the core of your career.
artistic.mid: You have a moderate interest in creative work. You enjoy adding your own ideas and style, but you also appreciate some structure. Roles that blend creativity with practical goals could suit you well, such as marketing specialist, content editor, interior adviser, UX designer, architect or teacher of a creative subject. Look for workplaces that give you room to suggest ideas while offering clear briefs and deadlines.
artistic.high: Artistic interests are your strongest area. You need room for imagination, originality and self-expression, and you dislike rigid routines. Example jobs: graphic designer, writer, journalist, musician, actor, photographer, illustrator, fashion designer, art director or game designer. You tend to thrive in flexible environments such as studios, agencies, media companies, theatres or as a freelancer, in roles where your ideas shape the result. Build a portfolio that shows your work, because in creative fields it often matters more than diplomas.

social.name: Social (The Helper)
social.short: Interest in helping, teaching, caring for and working with people.
social.low: Working closely with people is not your main source of motivation. You may prefer tasks, data, ideas or technical work over teaching, caring or counselling. Roles that revolve around constant contact and emotional support, such as nursing or social work, may drain you. Choose environments where you can focus on your work with limited interruptions, while keeping some contact with colleagues so you do not become isolated.
social.mid: You have a moderate interest in working with people. You enjoy helping and collaborating, but you also need time for your own tasks. Roles that combine people contact with a specialist focus could suit you, such as dental hygienist, HR adviser, trainer, librarian, customer success manager or occupational therapist. Look for workplaces where helping others is part of the job, but not every minute of it.
social.high: Social interests are your strongest area. You feel most fulfilled when helping, teaching, caring for or supporting people. Example jobs: teacher, nurse, social worker, psychologist, counsellor, coach, physiotherapist, HR professional, youth worker or care home manager. You tend to thrive in cooperative environments such as schools, hospitals, community organisations and non-profits, in roles where your work makes a direct difference to others. Protect your own energy, because caring jobs can be emotionally demanding.

enterprising.name: Enterprising (The Persuader)
enterprising.short: Interest in leading, persuading, selling and building businesses.
enterprising.low: Leading, selling and competing are not what motivate you. You likely prefer to focus on your own expertise, on people or on creative or careful work rather than on targets and persuasion. Jobs centred on sales, management or entrepreneurship may feel stressful or hollow to you. Look for roles where quality and expertise count more than influence, and where someone else handles the commercial side.
enterprising.mid: You have a moderate interest in enterprising work. You can take the lead or persuade others when needed, though you may not want commercial targets to dominate your job. Roles that combine expertise with influence could suit you, such as project lead, consultant, recruiter, events organiser or specialist team manager. Look for workplaces where you can grow into responsibility at your own pace.
enterprising.high: Enterprising interests are your strongest area. You enjoy leading, persuading, taking risks and chasing ambitious goals. Example jobs: entrepreneur, sales manager, business developer, marketing director, lawyer, real estate agent, politician, store manager or investment adviser. You tend to thrive in dynamic, competitive environments such as start-ups, corporate management, sales teams or your own business, in roles with responsibility, visibility and rewards for results. Pair your drive with good listening and ethical judgement.

conventional.name: Conventional (The Organiser)
conventional.short: Interest in organising, administration, data and clear procedures.
conventional.low: Organised, procedure-based work is not what energises you. You probably prefer variety, creativity, people or hands-on action over routine administration and detailed record keeping. Jobs built mainly on processing data, checking documents or following strict rules may feel confining. Seek out roles with variety and freedom, and use simple tools or a supportive colleague to handle the administrative tasks that every job brings.
conventional.mid: You have a moderate interest in conventional work. You appreciate order and accuracy, but you also want some variety. Roles that combine structure with other elements could suit you, such as office manager, paralegal, logistics planner, payroll specialist, medical secretary or project support officer. Look for workplaces that offer clear processes but also chances to improve them or work with people.
conventional.high: Conventional interests are your strongest area. You like order, accuracy, clear procedures and working with numbers or information. Example jobs: accountant, bookkeeper, auditor, administrator, data entry specialist, bank officer, logistics coordinator, compliance officer or archivist. You tend to thrive in structured environments such as offices, banks, government agencies and large organisations, in roles where reliability and precision are valued. Consider certifications that recognise your accuracy, and look for chances to design better systems.

summary: Your work interests fall into six types. Below you see how strongly each type shows up in your answers, with your strongest one highlighted as your main interest area. Most people fit a combination of two or three types, so look at your top scores together when exploring careers. Interests are only one part of a good career choice; skills, values and circumstances matter too.
